title: Judging and Grading every Fitness Channel (II: Jeff Nippard, Eric Bugenhagen...)
summary: Part 2 of NH's 200-point grading series: he explains his strict French-style grading, then grades Shredded Sports Science 137, Muscle Monsters 123, Jeff Nippard 150.5, Geoffrey Verity Schofield 147.5, CT Fletcher and Eric Bugenhagen 133. Recurring themes are integrity versus selling out, theory without practice, black-pilling, parasocial fanbases, supplement selling and clickbait.
claims: NH grades French-style: in a 0-20 system real grades run from about 5 to 15, so 150/200 is close to the practical maximum and 100 versus 150 is night and day
All criteria get equal weight (10 points) so as not to add subjectivity, even though NH thinks programming matters more

Shredded Sports Science scored 137/200: humor 9, production 10, conciseness 9.5, supplements 10, but experience 4 and physique 1 because he does not walk the walk, and usefulness 4 because it became a gossip channel
The experience you build yourself, empirical or anecdotal, is what is most valuable to share, because people can relate to it and trust it
Shredded Sports Science lost integrity points for refusing to call out a friend involved in a fraud scandal while constantly calling out others
Channels that only deconstruct must also rebuild; a few snippets of 'the right method' are not enough
Applying theory to everything without testing it against reality makes you dogmatic
Relentlessly negative exposé channels black-pill viewers: they destroy faith in the industry and in oneself, and while debunking PED standards they also lower natural standards
Recycling is only a problem when the audience can notice it; the biggest sin in show business is being boring

Muscle Monsters scored 123/200: basic content that keeps you in a hamster wheel, fine for your first year then outgrown; heavy clickbait (2), sells testosterone boosters (supplements 0), but 13 years on the platform
Once a fitness page passes a million subscribers it must choose between keeping its integrity and selling out to grow
Marketing a special method to gain 20 lb of muscle smells like a scam
Channels that put 'science' in titles and cite a single study for 15 seconds are using science as clickbait and should be punished
'Fitness schizophrenia': people look much better in thumbnails and photos than on video because they know how to market themselves

Jeff Nippard scored 150.5/200: the best programming channel on YouTube (9.5), integrity 9 and scandal-free, science 8 as a pioneer of science-based content, production 10; dogmatism 4, some dated hypertrophy ideas, and a supplement line with pre-workout
Experience scores cannot be very high for people in their 20s; age matters for experience
Most fitness creators who reach millions of subscribers lose their integrity
Big youtubers routinely change an underperforming video's title and thumbnail to something more clickbaity

Geoffrey Verity Schofield scored 147.5/200: programming-centred content (8.5), empathy 9, god complex 9, supplements 10; homemade production (6), a generalist, and a tendency to overrate his own genetics
Programming-focused content is what natural lifters need
Neither GVS nor NH has yet put in 10 years of hardcore lifting
Creators bigger than 99% of their viewers start believing they are genetically gifted and push that ideology; what they really have is mostly time and balls
As audiences demand studies over experience, channels drift toward citing science everywhere and risk losing authenticity; balance anecdotal and empirical evidence
To grow in fitness YouTube you have to clickbait; titles matter more than thumbnails
Most supplements are bogus scams pushed by influencers

CT Fletcher: programming 2, usefulness 2.5 (park bros would give better advice), integrity 4 over an obviously enhanced heart transplant and fat-burner sales; but dogmatism 10, parasocial 9, empathy 9
Someone who ruined his health with steroids up to about 300 lb and then got a heart transplant took a heart someone more deserving could have had
CT Fletcher was one of the first people NH followed when he started out as a young skinny lifter
Superfoods like African mango have no magical properties
Eric Bugenhagen scored 133/200: experience 10, originality 9.5, physique 9.5; programming 5.5 and usefulness 6 because he gives motivation without method; his fanboys are the worst
For novices, intensity-first methods like daily Bulgarian-style maxes get results; optimisation only works for people already sold on training
Programming advice that is all about intensity leads followers to believe intensity is the only variable
Motivation is the most important half, but you still need the method: without the pickaxe you break the rock with your forehead
When fans worship a creator as a god they come to believe they can never reach his level
NH disagrees with Bugenhagen's diet stance
NH plans 10 grading episodes in total, released monthly
exercises: work up to a 1RM every day
Bugenhagen's intensity-first method; works for novices
